> As AGJ60 says, I can of course go back and run the lm function just

> Furthermore, I'm wondering if I can gain access to all the data
> available. So if I facet the data, for example, I want the coefficients
> for each facet so I can make a comparison.

I think the point here is that ggplot is primarily designed for
building graphics, not for doing data summarization and analysis. It
does the latter in order to do its job, but learning how to use the
other tools that Hadley has written (plyr, reshape[2], ...) is in the
long run likely to be more productive than trying to dig all the answers
out of ggplot.

messages.author: cbb02003b224e313
messages.subject: Extracting Statistics
parts:
Hey all,

I just began using ggplot2 a few weeks ago, and I'm loving it. I have
one major question though. If I create a smoothing line or curve, say
a linear regression line, is there any way to get the coefficients
out? I realize this is a graphing package, but being that ggplot2
clearly runs the statistics to plot the curves, it would be wonderful
to have access to the numerical results so I don't have to go back and
duplicate work. I've done some googling, and looked around the user
manual quite a bit, and I haven't been able to find anything, so
hopefully I'm not asking a question that's already been answered.

Thanks!

~Mike

messages.author: 27405c4b711a1080
messages.subject: Re: Extracting Statistics
parts:
Mike, 

I do believe you can get the numbers out of the ggplot2/grid object, but I think you can do them much easier outside of ggplot2. (Do a google groups search on "extract" and "stat" and something probably comes up)

The procedures that the stat functions do vary and you have some flexibility in, for example, choosing which function will linearly model your data or the degree of error (I think there was an email that said the default was 95% CI the other day).  

It would be nice if this information was centralized and a list of options was given. Always nice to know your options. I know that Hadley and a student/postdoc are working on improving documentation for the next release. 

I'm sorry that's not terribly helpful, but hopefully someone who knows more will chime in and fill you in. 

Brandon

messages.author: daf017f67eba24e8
messages.subject: Re: Extracting Statistics
parts:
yes, i've used it alot. i am a bit nervous that takahashi says it's not guaranteed to be included with future releases of ggplot. I do agree it's best to calculate your stats outside of ggplot if they are critical or important and then useing stat_identity to plot them, but often getting at what ggplot calculated is really practical (reduces effort duplication) and can even be used to make the plot better (for example adding labels in just the right locations which result from stats). 

without looking at an actual example, i believe it only gives the data used in the plot... ie how your stat translates into a graphic. so you're only basically pulling the data off the plot with this approach.... but i could be wrong, it might give more detail. you have to look around inside the object returned by ggplot_build, it's a bit of groping in the dark..

str() doesnt usually give much on functions, try just 

ggplot_build

James
